When the author wrote one entry for two or more compounds and printed each of their labels, copy the whole printed string as it stands -- `9a and 9b` -- rather than choosing one. null when the unit is about no compound the author named, and always null for the other kinds.

kind.description: NARRATIVE is the argument: introduction, results and discussion, conclusion, and the abstract. GENERAL_METHODS is the experimental part's preface: instruments, solvents, purification, how spectra were recorded. PROCEDURE is one compound's preparation. CHARACTERIZATION is one compound's data. CRYSTALLOGRAPHY is X-ray work -- crystal data, refinement, atomic coordinates, bond lengths and angles, displacement parameters -- which usually runs for pages and is one unit per structure, labelled with the compound crystallized. BIBLIOGRAPHY is the reference list, whatever the journal calls it and however it numbers it: where the author printed it as one run it is one unit from its first entry to its last, and where the journal prints the citations as numbered notes at the foot of each page, each run of consecutive citation blocks is a unit of its own, because the prose between them belongs to other units. What makes one of those notes part of it is that it cites a work -- authors, title, journal, year. A numbered note that instead says something about this work ("diastereomers were separable, but only separated once") is not a reference and is not BIBLIOGRAPHY, whatever number it carries. Do not read past the references for the document's chemistry unless there is a procedure printed after them, which does happen when a supplement is bound into the same file. OTHER is what none of these are: title and authors, affiliations, dates received, table of contents, acknowledgements, notes on the supporting information, copies of spectra, and a screening table dumped as text.
